newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: COWLEY SAYS MEDIA COMPANIES SHOULD OPERATE AS THEY WISH
News Limited executive chairman Ken Cowley says Australia shouldn't be "precious" about its cross-media and foriegn-ownership laws.
In Cairns last night, Mr Cowley said the federal government shouldn't interfere, rather let Australian and overseas companies operate as they wish.
And Mr Cowley raised concerns about an alleged "deal" between the government and rival Kerry Packer over media ownership.
He says he's concerned there have been commitments to have cross media done by some ministers.
VANSTONE TO GO TO NEWCASTLE
The Federal Employment Minister will become the fourth Federal Minister to visit Newcastle today, when she goes there to discuss how her department can assist BHP workers who'll be made redundant.
BHP is to close its steelmaking in the area in 1999.
Senator Vanstone will hold talks this morning with BHP's transition committee, chaired by Group general manager of the Long Products Division, Bob Kirkby.
The group was set up to assist with the transition of BHP workers into other employment.
Two-and-a-half thousand jobs will go when steelmaking ends, with a BHP survey showing that between 800 and 1000 workers are expected to be unemployed.
WHYALLA BHP WORKERS TO MEET THIS MORNING
B-H-P workers at Whyalla will meet this morning to discuss a possible 24-hour strike.
Workers at most other B-H-P steel sites went on strike last week.
The A-C-T-U has called for strike action in protest against the company's decision to end steelmaking at Newcastle.
Unions involved also want the Federal Government to develop an industry and regional development policy.
BORBIDGE ALL BUT ACCEPTS 10-POINT PLAN
The Queensland Premier has backed away from his hardline position against the Prime Minister's 10-point plan, saying his Government will have to work within the framework drafted by Canberra.
Rob Borbidge says it provides the states with flexibility for dealing with claims over pastoral leases and is more workable than it was originally.
Mr Borbidge says it's not his preferred position, and he still wants to see draft legislation to ensure it can deliver as much certainty of title to pastoralists as possible.
He claims John Howard has made some concessions in some areas, but only because of pressure placed on him by Queensland.
QANTAS STAFF MAY TAKE INDUSTRIAL ACTION OVER TENDERING
The Australian Services Union is not ruling out future industrial action by Qantas ground staff over moves to introduce competitive tendering in three states.
Qantas plans to call tenders on Friday for customer service and ramp work at Perth, Melbourne and Brisbane airports.
The union will today meet with about a thousand workers in the three cities, worried about massive job losses.
Qantas says it's not expecting disruption today and it's starting talks with the union.
A representative says the company will consult unions and comply with a competitive tendering protocol in an enterprise bargaining agreement.
The Industrial Relations Commission in Sydney has ordered both parties to form a steering committee to examine the impact of contracting out services.
TASMANIAN MINISTER SAYS FIREBLIGHT STRETCHES CREDIBILITY
Tasmania's Primary Industry Minister says a second suspected discovery of fireblight disease in Australia by a New Zealand scientist stretches credibility to its limit.
The Minister, Bill Bonde, says there is strong prima facie evidence of highly unethical behaviour by some New Zealand individuals.
He says New Zealand should welcome a national investigation announced by the Federal Government into the appearance of fireblight in Australia to clear them of any suspicion.
Mr Bonde says it stretches the imagination to believe the discovery of the disease in both the Adelaide and Melbourne Botanical Gardens by New Zealand scientists is coincidental.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
